procedural_history.originating_court: Trial Court (inferred from 'Original Suit No. 266 of 2004' and 'Original Suit No. 112 of 2003')
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgments of the High Court dated 08th August 2011 and 03rd February 2012 (Civil Appeals), and judgments dated 28.10.2008 and 30th (Criminal Appeals)
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Original Suit No. 112 of 2003 and Original Suit No. 266 of 2004 were dismissed vide judgment dated 06th January 2004 and 29th July 2005 respectively. Appeals were preferred before the High Court. The Appeals against the judgments in criminal matters were allowed by the High Court vide common judgment and order of conviction and sentence dated 28.10.2008 and 30th
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Appeals against the judgments of the High Court are before the Supreme Court to be disposed of via a common judgment. The Civil Appeals challenge the judgments dated 08th August 2011 and 03rd February 2012 passed by the Madras High Court whereby the Original Suits filed by the plaintiff- respondents for recovery of money on the basis of promissory notes were decreed.

directions: The judgments and orders dated 10th July 2011 passed by the Trial Court is confirmed.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was correct in concluding, based on the preponderance of probability, that the plaintiff had the financial ability to lend a sum of Rs. 3 lakhs.

facts: In the civil proceedings, unlike the related criminal case, the plaintiff successfully proved the existence of the promissory notes.
The High Court found that the plaintiff had established he worked as a LIC agent and derived agricultural income from his father's extensive properties.
The High Court also noted that the defendants/appellants failed to examine the appellant's wife as a witness to support their defence.
The defendants/appellants argued that the plaintiff lacked financial capacity, pointing to Income Tax Returns that did not declare the loan or the agricultural income.
law: The standard of proof in civil proceedings is the "preponderance of probabilities," which is different from the standard in criminal proceedings.
The principle of adverse inference can be applied against a party that withholds the best available evidence (in this case, the testimony of the appellant's wife).
application: The Supreme Court observed that the High Court correctly decided the civil appeals based on the standard of preponderance of probabilities.
The High Court weighed the evidence and concluded that the plaintiff's income from being a LIC agent and from agriculture was sufficient to establish his financial ability to lend Rs. 3 lakhs.
The High Court also drew an adverse inference against the defendants/appellants for not examining the appellant's wife, which weakened their defence.
The Supreme Court distinguished the civil case from the criminal case, noting that the promissory notes were proven in the civil suit and the standard of proof is lower.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court found no reason to interfere with the High Court's judgment in the civil appeals. It upheld the High Court's conclusion, which was based on the preponderance of probability, that the plaintiff had the financial ability to lend the sum of Rs. 3 lakhs. The Supreme Court effectively rejected the appellant's challenge to this finding.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in drawing an adverse inference against the defendants/appellants for not examining the appellant's wife as a witness, on the grounds that the best available evidence was withheld.

facts: In the civil proceedings, the defendants/appellants put forward a defense plea to counter the plaintiff's claim for recovery of money.
The appellant's wife was a party to the initial transactions but was not examined as a witness by the defendants/appellants to support or 'probabilize' their defense.
law: The standard of proof in civil proceedings is the "preponderance of probabilities."
A court may draw an adverse inference against a party if it finds that the party has withheld the best available evidence.
application: The Supreme Court noted that the High Court had decided the civil appeals based on the standard of preponderance of probabilities.
The High Court found that the failure of the defendants/appellants to examine the appellant's wife as a witness amounted to withholding the best available evidence.
Based on this failure, the High Court applied the principle of adverse inference against the defendants/appellants.
This adverse inference was one of the factors, along with the plaintiff proving the promissory notes and his financial capacity, that led the High Court to its conclusion.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court found no reason to interfere with the judgment of the High Court in the civil appeals. By upholding the High Court's decision, the Supreme Court implicitly agreed that the High Court was justified in drawing an adverse inference against the appellants for not examining the appellant's wife, as this was considered a withholding of the best available evidence to support their defense.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was correct in concluding, based on the preponderance of probability, that the plaintiff had the financial ability to lend a sum of Rs. 3 lakhs.
appellant_arguments: The respondents (plaintiffs) did not have the financial capacity to lend Rs. 3,00,000.

Although the respondents claimed the funds came from agricultural income, they had not declared this income in their tax returns from 1992-1999, meaning there was no material evidence to prove their financial capacity.
respondent_arguments: The plaintiff had the financial ability to lend the sum, and this was established by the evidence on record based on the standard of preponderance of probability.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in drawing an adverse inference against the defendants/appellants for not examining the appellant's wife as a witness, on the grounds that the best available evidence was withheld.
appellant_arguments: The High Court was not justified in drawing an adverse inference for the non-examination of the appellant's wife.
respondent_arguments: An adverse inference was correctly drawn against the appellants because their failure to examine the appellant's wife amounted to withholding the best available evidence.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The adjudication in civil matters is based on a preponderance of probabilities, whereas in criminal cases, the accused is presumed innocent and guilt must be proven beyond all reasonable doubt.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Supreme Court rejected the High Court's reasoning and overturned its judgment, restoring the Trial Court's original order which had dismissed the plaintiff's suits. The Supreme Court found that the High Court was incorrect in its conclusion that the plaintiff had established the financial ability to lend the sum of Rs. 3 lakhs. It also held that the High Court was not justified in drawing an adverse inference against the defendants for the non-examination of a witness.
legal_tests_applied: Preponderance of Probability: The standard of proof in civil matters, which the High Court applied to conclude that the plaintiff had the financial ability to lend the money. The Supreme Court found this application to be erroneous.

Adverse Inference for Withholding Evidence: The principle that a negative inference can be drawn if a party withholds the best available evidence. The High Court applied this against the defendants for not examining the appellant's wife as a witness, a finding the Supreme Court rejected as unjustified.
why_appellant_lost: The High Court drew an adverse inference against the defendants/appellants for not examining the appellant's wife as a witness, concluding that they had withheld the best available evidence.
why_respondent_won: The High Court, applying the standard of preponderance of probability to the evidence on record, concluded that the plaintiff had the financial ability to lend the sum of Rs. 3 lakhs.
